Orchot Tzadikim 12:21: When a person is fasting, or in some kind of trouble, anger is then very strong in his heart. Therefore at such times one must be especially careful not to become angry. Silence nullifies anger, and a low voice also nullifies anger. Therefore, when a person sees his anger growing powerful over him, let him be silent or speak gently, and not raise his voice in his anger; for whoever raises his voice at the time of his anger only arouses the anger further, while a low voice and silence quiet the anger. He should also avoid looking at the face of a person he is angry at, but speak with him without looking at his face, and this will drive the anger from his heart.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:22: And know that the completeness of a person's intellect lies in ruling over his anger, as it is said (Proverbs 19:11), "the intelligence of a man makes him slow to anger." Anger tends strongly toward pride, and no angry person escapes pride; and you already know the evils of pride. It is fitting for a person to keep far from anger; and even in a matter where it would be justified to be angry, he should restrain his spirit and not be angry. And this is how one prone to anger should act from the start, when he first resolves not to be angry: he must not feel anger at all — even if struck and cursed, he should not become agitated or take notice.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:23: And this is a clear matter: whoever is very impatient finds it easier to feel nothing at all — to be silent and completely restrain his spirit from becoming even slightly angry, for it is impossible for the angry man to allow himself to become only a little angry; for if he lets even a little anger take hold in his heart, in the end he will become very angry. And whoever wishes to restrain his spirit from anger, yet also wishes to cast dread upon the members of his household — and if he is a communal leader and wishes to be angry at the community so that they return to the good path — how should he act? He should show himself before them as though he is angry, in order to discipline them, while his own mind remains settled between himself and himself — like a person who pretends to be angry at the time of his anger, but is not actually angry. And when he displays his anger, he should be careful not to do so when he has poor guests, for they will suppose he is angry at them; therefore he should show himself joyful before them.
Orchot Tzadikim 12:24: Our Sages commanded that one distance himself from anger, to the point of training himself not to feel anything even at things that anger him, until he uproots anger from his heart entirely — and this is a good path. And the way of the righteous is this: they are insulted and do not insult, they hear their own disgrace and do not answer, and they rejoice in sufferings. And of them the verse says (Judges 5:31), "and they who love Him shall be as the sun going forth in its might" (Shabbat 88b).
Orchot Tzadikim 13:2: Goodwill. This is a very good trait, and it is found only in a generous and precious soul. Whoever has the trait of goodwill is content in all his affairs, according to whatever the exalted Creator decrees for him, and does not question it. And whoever possesses this trait does not look toward greatness or honor, but his will and his mind are to bear things patiently; and he does not complain about his affairs, nor is he angry with the exalted Lord, saying, "why has the Blessed Lord done such-and-such?" And included in this trait is one who rejoices in his own portion. And you already know the virtue and greatness of this trait.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:3: And when a righteous person is favorably disposed toward people, and people are favorably disposed toward him, the Omnipresent too is favorably disposed toward him. And even his enemies make peace with him, as it is written (Proverbs 16:7), "when the Lord is pleased with a man's ways, He makes even his enemies be at peace with him." And so you know from Abimelech's favor toward Abraham, and how they made peace with one another (Bereishit Rabbah 54:1). And it is said (Proverbs 16:15), "in the light of the king's face is life, and his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:4: See what happened to Mordechai when Ahasuerus favored him, and what happened to Joseph when Pharaoh favored him. If such greatness comes to one whom people favor, how much greater must be the level of one whom the Holy One, blessed be He, favors! Therefore let a person exert himself to perform the commandments, and then the Blessed Lord will favor him. And the wise man said: whoever has this trait will grow rich. And from the trait of goodwill comes forgiveness and pardon, that one be reconciled to whoever has wronged him and overlook the wrong, for whoever overlooks wrongs done to him has his prayer heard.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:5: It is a very, very fine trait for a person to be full of goodwill, setting aside his own opinion in deference to his fellow's opinion. And this brings it about that he is beloved by all, when he does what is agreeable to each and every person. And such a person is very close to the paths of teshuvah, for when he is caught up in an evil deed and his fellow comes to rebuke him, he agrees at once to abandon the evil and returns to the good. It follows that he has satisfaction in himself when he admits and abandons his evil ways, and his companions who associate with him have satisfaction as well.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:6: And so Solomon said (Proverbs 12:15), "but he who listens to counsel is wise" — this does not mean mere hearing with the ear, but rather "listens" means that he heeds the counsel of the wise and agrees to do as the wise man tells him. It follows that the entire Torah is contained within the trait of goodwill, and likewise all rebukes and all blessings. How so? At the time of the giving of the Torah it is written (Exodus 19:5), "and now, if you will indeed obey (shamoa tishme'u) My voice and keep My covenant, then you shall be My own treasure from among all peoples." This is the meaning of "obey, obey": that you accept it upon yourselves and agree willingly. And they answered, "we will do and we will hear" (ibid. verse 8) — meaning they agreed.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:7: Regarding the curses it is said (Deuteronomy 28:15), "and it shall come to pass, if you will not hearken to the voice of the Lord your God, to observe to do all His commandments and His statutes"; and it is written (Deuteronomy 11:27-28), "the blessing, if you obey the commandments of the Lord your God... and the curse, if you do not obey the commandments of the Lord your God..." And all these "hearings" do not mean mere hearing with the ear, but rather mean that one agrees to do. And so we find with Jacob our father, peace upon him, who agreed with his mother and heeded her counsel regarding the blessings, and agreed to heed his father and his mother and took a wife at their instruction — therefore he merited that twelve tribes came forth from him. And it is written (Proverbs 1:33), "but he who listens to me shall dwell securely, and shall be at ease from fear of evil."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:8: There are four kinds of listening: there is one who listens and loses; one who listens and gains; one who does not listen and gains; and one who does not listen and loses. "Listens and loses" — this is Adam, of whom it is said (Genesis 3:17), "and to Adam He said: because you have listened to the voice of your wife." And what did he lose? As it is said (ibid.), "for dust you are, and to dust you shall return."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:9: "Listens and gains" — this is Abraham our father, to whom it was said (Genesis 21:12), "whatever Sarah says to you, listen to her voice." And what did he gain? As it was said to him (ibid.), "for in Isaac shall your seed be called."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:10: "Does not listen and gains" — this is Joseph, of whom it is said (Genesis 39:10), "and he did not listen to her, to lie beside her, to be with her." And what did he gain? "And Joseph, he was the ruler over the land" (ibid. 42:6).
Orchot Tzadikim 13:11: "Does not listen and loses" — this is Israel, of whom it is said (Jeremiah 7:26), "and they did not listen to Me, nor incline their ear." And what did they lose? "Such as are for death, to death; and such as are for the sword, to the sword" (ibid. 15:2); and it is said (Isaiah 1:19), "if you be willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:12: The wayward and rebellious son is put to death because he did not listen, as it is written (Deuteronomy 21:19-21), "then his father and his mother shall take hold of him, and bring him out to the elders of his city, and to the gate of his place, and they shall say to the elders of his city: this our son is wayward and rebellious, he will not listen to our voice, he is a glutton and a drunkard. And all the men of his city shall stone him."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:13: And of all Israel it is said (Deuteronomy 9:7), "you were rebellious against the Lord." And it is further written of their unwillingness to listen (Exodus 34:9), "for it is a stiff-necked people."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:14: And since everything depends on the trait of goodwill, one should direct all his will toward doing the commandments of the Blessed Lord. And so our Sages said (Avot 2:4): do His will as your own will, so that He will do your will as His own will.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:15: In sum: a person should not be obstinate, nor harden his neck against those who rebuke him and against one who shows him the straight path; rather, he should be favorably disposed toward them, and accept their words willingly. For of the obstinate it is said (Proverbs 22:5), "thorns and snares are in the way of the obstinate; he who guards his soul shall stay far from them"; and it is said (ibid. 17:20), "he who has a perverse heart finds no good." And in several places those who desire to heed the words of Torah are praised, as it is written (Psalms 1:2-3), "but his delight is in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditates day and night; and he shall be like a tree planted by streams of water, that brings forth its fruit in its season." And it is written (ibid. 112:1), "happy is the man who fears the Lord, who greatly delights in His commandments" — it says only "delights," meaning that a person should set his desire upon the commandments.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:16: Rabbi Abahu said: in the future, everyone will be astonished at one who listened to God, and will say: who is this, that so-and-so, who did not read Scripture and did not study, yet sits with the Patriarchs and converses with them? And God will say to them: why are you astonished? These merited it only because they listened to Me, as it is said (Proverbs 15:31), "the ear that listens to the reproof of life shall abide among the wise."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:17: Even though this trait is very good, one should not use it toward the wicked, and should not be agreeable to them; rather, he should remove his goodwill from all bad things, and from all that the Torah has warned him against. Rather, let him be agreeable to whomever the Holy One, blessed be He, favors, as it is written (Psalms 147:11), "the Lord favors those who fear Him."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:18: And he should set his goodwill upon the commandments, even though they are very hard for him — he should set his goodwill upon them until they become dear to him. For even though it was hard in the eyes of Abraham our father, peace upon him, to slaughter his only son, he set aside his own will for the sake of the will of the exalted Creator, and rose early and acted with alacrity, with a willing soul and with love.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:19: But whoever sets his will and his desire upon bad deeds, and is agreeable toward the wicked and their deeds, and despises the righteous — that very goodwill brings him down to the depths of Sheol. And of them it is said (Isaiah 5:20), "woe to those who call evil good, and good evil"; and it is said (Proverbs 17:15), "he who justifies the wicked, and he who condemns the righteous, both of them alike are an abomination to the Lord."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:20: Whoever wishes to enter into the depth of piety and the depth of [God's] unity, to know the Blessed Lord, can only do so if he is wise, understanding, and of a willing soul without anger. It is written (Proverbs 8:32), "now therefore, children, listen to me, and happy are they who keep my ways." The Blessed Creator said to Israel: I ask of you only that you listen to Me. If you listen to Me, I will fulfill what the prophets prophesied: "if you be willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land" (Isaiah 1:19), and it is written (Proverbs 8:34), "happy is the man who listens to me."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:21: Therefore let a person set his mind on the will of the Blessed Creator, and not rebel against his teachers and against whoever is greater than he. And so it is said in the Torah (Deuteronomy 17:9-12), "and you shall come to the priests, the Levites, and to the judge who shall be in those days, and inquire, and they shall declare to you the sentence of judgment. And you shall act according to what they declare to you... you shall not turn aside from what they declare to you, to the right hand or to the left. And the man who acts presumptuously, not listening to the priest who stands to minister there before the Lord your God, or to the judge, that man shall die, and you shall put away the evil from Israel."
Orchot Tzadikim 13:22: From all of this we learn how great is the trait of goodwill, that the entire Torah is contained within it. Even if the Sages tell you that the left is the right, and the right is the left, you should be agreeable to listen to them (Sifrei, Devarim 17:11).
Orchot Tzadikim 13:23: Consider that we pray in our prayers: "and may the service of Israel Your people always be favorably accepted." Behold, all our deeds and our service depend entirely on the goodwill of the Blessed Creator. And at a time a person does not set his will and his desire upon the commandments of the exalted Lord, but rebels against Him, and chooses the bad deeds that the Blessed Lord has warned him not to do — how will the Blessed Lord be favorably disposed toward that man? How can He favor and desire a man who does not favor and desire Him?
Orchot Tzadikim 13:24: And a person should never be obstinate against the Blessed Creator and his teachers, for one sage was praised for this: in all my days I never disregarded the words of my colleagues! I myself know I am not a priest, yet if my colleagues told me, "go up to the platform [to bless the people]!" I would go up (Shabbat 118b).
Orchot Tzadikim 13:25: And there is no need to elaborate on this trait, for it is contained within the trait of love and the trait of joy.
Orchot Tzadikim 13:26: There is nothing in the world as good as listening. And so they said (Shemot Rabbah 27:9): a person fell from the roof and broke his limbs — he needs a compress and a bandage for each and every one of his limbs and bones. But the sinner, who sins with all his limbs, of whom it is said (Isaiah 1:6), "from the sole of the foot even to the head there is no soundness in it" — behold, the Blessed Lord heals all his limbs with a single compress, and that is the listening of the ear, as it is said (ibid. 55:3), "incline your ear, and come to Me; listen, and your soul shall live."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:2: Envy is a branch of anger, and no person is entirely free of it, for we see that all people are drawn one after another: when a person sees that his fellow has acquired some possession in worldly matters — whether kinds of food, kinds of clothing, or if he builds a house or gathers money — he then exerts himself to obtain the same, for he thinks: my fellow has this, so shall I have it too. And this matter King Solomon hinted at (Ecclesiastes 4:4), "and I saw all labor and all skillful work, that it comes from a man's envy of his neighbor."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:3: Whoever is overpowered by this trait is very disgraceful. For envy leads to covetousness, since when a person does not take to heart and does not envy what others possess, he does not covet; but when he lets his heart be drawn and envies what others possess, he then covets. And the Torah said (Exodus 20:14), "you shall not covet." And when he covets, he then robs, as it is written (Micah 2:2), "and they covet fields and rob them." And a person in whom covetousness grows powerful is close to transgressing all Ten Commandments. There is a story of a man who had a wicked neighbor, with a wall separating between them. And the wicked man coveted his neighbor's wife and some of his possessions. One day, on the eve of the Sabbath, he heard the man say to his wife, "I wish to go out on a business trip," and so he did. What did that wicked man do? He went on the Sabbath night and broke through the wall that separated between them — behold, he transgressed "remember the Sabbath day to keep it holy." He went and forced himself upon the woman he coveted, and lay with her — behold, he transgressed "you shall not commit adultery." Afterward, when he began to rob the money, the woman cried out, and he rose against her to kill her — behold, he transgressed "you shall not murder." And when he stole and robbed what he coveted — behold, he transgressed "you shall not steal" and "you shall not covet." The next day his father and mother stood up and rebuked him; he rose against them and struck them — behold, he transgressed "honor your father and your mother." Afterward he was brought before the court, and he and a wicked companion testified that these possessions he had taken were a pledge belonging to him, held in pledge from the woman's husband, and they believed him, and he could not be made to return them, until it came out that robbers had broken through the wall between them and killed the woman, and when the husband heard of the killing, he too entered and took his pledge back — behold, he transgressed "you shall not answer [falsely]." And wherever he went, he swore that he had done no wrong at all — behold, he transgressed "you shall not take [God's name in vain]." In the end his wickedness was revealed and his crime became known, and out of shame he took to a life of wickedness and denied the living God — behold, he transgressed "I am the Lord your God." And in the end he became devoted to idolatry and bowed down to it — behold, he transgressed "you shall have no other gods before Me" and "you shall not bow down to them nor serve them." And all this was brought about by covetousness. It follows that whoever covets is close to transgressing the entire Torah.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:4: But there is another way to understand and grasp how very corrupt envy and covetousness are. It is along the path Solomon, peace upon him, spoke (Proverbs 23:17), "let not your heart envy sinners, but [continue] in the fear of the Lord all the day." When a person envies sinners and sees their wealth and their success, and sees the righteous impoverished and afflicted with sufferings, his soul may thereby come to be disgusted with the fear of God and His judgments and statutes, and he may come to despise those who study Torah and fulfill it, as the matter is said (Malachi 3:13-15), "your words have been stout against Me, says the Lord. Yet you say, what have we spoken against You? You have said, it is vain to serve God; and what profit is it that we have kept His charge, and that we have walked mournfully before the Lord of Hosts? And now we call the proud happy; those who work wickedness are built up; even those who tempt God are delivered."
Orchot Tzadikim 14:5: And this path brings folly into people's minds, and turns their hearts backward when they see the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer; and through this they walk according to the wantonness of their own hearts and say: so-and-so and so-and-so do such-and-such, and they are rich — so let us do the same, and whatever happens to them will happen to us too! And all this comes from envy — envying the wicked and coveting their wealth and their ease — and because of this they cast off the yoke of the commandments from themselves. But the righteous do not envy the wicked, and do not covet their money or their ease, for they think that their wealth is preserved for their own harm, and their ease is meant to destroy them from out of the great good hidden away for the righteous. And they think that the poverty and distress of the righteous are meant to refine and purify them, and to increase their level for the World to Come. There is no doubt: whoever thinks this way will not covet or envy; rather, he will rejoice upon seeing the ease of the wicked, and say: if it is thus for those who anger Him, how much more so will He give, and give again, to those who do His will!
Orchot Tzadikim 14:6: Envy comes from a deficiency of the soul. If a person envies another's beauty, or his strength, or his wealth, behold, he does not desire what the Blessed Creator has decreed for him. And this is like a servant who has complaints about his master's actions and is not agreeable regarding his master's affairs — this is not a faithful servant. How much more so is there no cause to complain against the Blessed Creator, all of whose deeds are upright and straight, and whom one should never suspect.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:7: From envy comes strife, as you see with Korach, who envied the honor of Elitzafan ben Uzziel, and through this he and his faction perished, even the nursing infants (Bamidbar Rabbah 18). Envy is to people like a disease of the body, and it brings on consumption. The wise man said to his son: guard yourself from envy, for it is recognizable in you — your face changes because of the evil in your heart. And the very man you envy rejoices at your heart's distress. Why should you make your enemy rejoice, and let him take revenge on you?
Orchot Tzadikim 14:8: The envious man robs his own soul, for he is constantly mourning and his intellect is diminished. And out of the great envy hidden within him, his heart has no room to study, or to pray with intent, or to do good deeds.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:9: Every person finds a pleasant taste in his food, except the envious man, who tastes no good taste in his food until the good fortune departs from his fellow.
Orchot Tzadikim 14:10: For every hatred there is hope: if he hates his fellow because he robbed him, the hatred will depart when the robbed item is returned to him. So too, every hatred that depends on some matter will cease once that matter is set right — except for one who hates his fellow because of envy. The wise man said to his son: do not envy your brother for what he has, for he will enjoy his life, while you will be filled with worry and grief. And the wise man said: the envious and covetous man was created only to be angry.
